description: "Lắng" (Listen to Explore - Feel the Universe) turns NASA data into sound and touch, making climate info accessible for the visually impaired and seniors in Vietnam (vital for typhoon alerts like Yagi). Using 20 NASA datasets, the app maps data to traditional instruments (đàn bầu for temperature, t'rưng for rainfall, flute for elevation) and vibrations for terrain, offering high-precision offline exploration of Earth, Moon, and Mars.
summary:
NASA’s Earth Information Center turns satellite data into images of night lights, lightning and carbon dioxide. Yet these images leave out blind people, older adults with poor eyesight and children who cannot read yet. Challenge 14 asks teams to pair such frames with real-time sound, and Team Lắng’s Earth Jukebox does exactly that.

Lắng uses five NASA SVS visualizations: night lights, ISS lightning, CO₂, sea temperature and GEDI forest height. It converts each frame’s colours back into numbers and plays them on Vietnamese folk instruments. Pitch shows the value, beats show the area affected, and stereo shows west or east.

Everything works by voice or touch. Users can say “nghe sét” (play lightning) or “năm 2020”, slide a finger over an image or terrain map to hear what lies beneath it, or draw a Z to return home. The same controls lead into space, with ten Solar System bodies, ten NASA recordings and four voice games. Lắng runs on the web and on Android, where speech and climate history work offline.

The sounds reveal real patterns: Vietnam’s night lights grew 44% from 2012 to 2023, against 17% globally, and lightning over Vietnam peaks in May, two months before the global peak
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lắng (https://lang-app-woad.vercel.app/) is a voice-controlled globe for people who cannot read a chart: blind and low-vision people, older adults with poor eyesight, and children who cannot read yet. Users speak in Vietnamese or English, a tone confirms each command, and a voice answers, so nothing on the screen has to be seen.

  1. Earth Jukebox (the core of Challenge 14). Five NASA SVS / Earth Information Center visualizations are played as sound: Black Marble night lights (SVS 5475), ISS LIS lightning (SVS 5011), GEOS CO₂ (SVS 5436/5196), ECCO2 sea-surface temperature (SVS 3912), and GEDI forest height (SVS 4950). Each opens with a spoken description of the image. Pitch follows the value, percussion density follows the area affected, stereo follows west to east, and a gong marks a clear change over Vietnam. Users can say “year 2020” to jump, “explain” to hear why a sound was chosen, or slide a finger over the image to hear each region. Vietnam’s night lights grew about 44% from 2012 to 2023, against 17% globally, and lightning over Vietnam peaks in May, two months before the global peak.
  2. Hear the climate. Temperature plays on the đàn bầu (one-string zither) and rain on the t’rưng (bamboo xylophone), using NASA GISTEMP v4 (146 years; 2024 was +1.28 °C above 1951–1980), NASA POWER for 34 provinces (1981–2025), 15-day replays of Typhoon Yagi and the 2020 Central Vietnam floods, and 282 disasters from NASA SEDAC GDIS.
  3. Touch the land. On a real terrain map, a flute rises with SRTM elevation, the phone vibrates with slope, and MODIS land cover adds water, forest, and town sounds.
  4. Explore space. NSSDCA planetary data, NASA Space Place facts, ten historical NASA recordings, and four voice-only games.

HOW IT WORKS

  • Data: A Python pipeline downloads, converts, validates, and compresses NASA data, with a data card for every file. For the Jukebox, build_eic.py turns each video frame into a $64 \times 32$ grid of values, using a method suited to each visualization (brightness, colour-bar matching, base-map subtraction, seasonal phase detection, or reprojection).
  • App: Flutter for Android, Windows, and the web; offline speech recognition with sherpa-onnx and Silero; offline Vietnamese voice with Piper; and instruments played on the device with flutter_soloud. Values are mapped to a pentatonic scale, and the exact number is always read aloud.
  • Accessibility: No screen needed; “stop”, “go back”, or a Z gesture work everywhere; high-contrast interface; offline on Android.
  • AI: Open questions go to Gemma 4 or Gemini, which always receives the relevant NASA data first, so it answers from the data rather than inventing numbers.

HOW WE CHECKED IT

After compressing 300 months of NASA POWER data, the largest error is 0.058 °C (temperature) and 1.485 mm/month (rain); our 2024 GISTEMP value matches NASA's; Đà Lạt reads 1,492 m against about 1,500 m in reality; about 3,900 automated tests run in CI on every push, including more than 3,300 voice-command sentences. While validating, we found that NASA POWER's long series for Vietnam has jumps over time (Hà Nội showed −0.97 °C cooling vs +1.02 °C warming in ERA5), so long-term trends use the ERA5 reanalysis and the app names that source aloud.

USER TESTING & FEEDBACK

(Survey conducted at 10:33 today with 171 participants evaluating usability and accessibility across core features)

  • Ease of Use: Rated an average of 4.40 / 5.0 for initial onboarding and ease of starting.
  • Instrument Sonification: Traditional instruments (đàn bầu, t'rưng, flute) received an average score of 4.31 / 5.0 for helping users intuitively understand scientific data.
  • Voice Clarity & Tactile Feedback: Voice clarity and map touch feedback scored 4.50 / 5.0 and 4.49 / 5.0 respectively.
  • User Retention & Impact: Willingness to use the app again averaged 4.55 / 5.0, and willingness to recommend Lắng to visually impaired individuals, seniors, and young children reached 4.61 / 5.0. The most popular features among testers were Voice Control (45%) and Space Exploration (27%).

LIMITS WE STATE OPENLY

NASA POWER cells are about 50 km; Earth Jukebox values are read from image colours and are approximate (sea temperature may read 1–2 °C high); the fire-season figures are still illustrative. While initial user testing shows strong positive feedback on usability and sound intuitiveness, broader validation with specialized blind associations is ongoing.

BENEFITS AND GOALS

A blind person can check this afternoon's rain, hear how bad past floods were, and feel the land around them without asking anyone. Children can learn climate and space by ear.

Next steps: Expand testing with Vietnamese blind associations, add an easy-listening mode, fix gesture conflicts with screen readers, and add live storm alerts from NASA EONET.
dataRefs: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio / Earth Information Center: SVS 5475 & 5313 (Black Marble VIIRS night lights), SVS 5011 (Lightning Imaging Sensor on the ISS), SVS 5436 & 5196 (GEOS DYAMOND CO₂), SVS 3912 (ECCO2 sea-surface temperature and currents), SVS 4950 (GEDI forest canopy height)
